power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

info.title: Diversity in the amount of information search and collective accuracy

author.affiliation:
Institute of Library, Information and Media Science
								University of Tsukuba

text.text: Individuals differ in how much information they acquire before deciding.
How does this heterogeneity affect collective accuracy when groups have the same total search resources?
We examined twentymember groups using an extension of a cue-based decision model.
Agents independently inspected assigned numbers of randomly selected binary cues, integrated them with equal weights, and combined their decisions by majority vote.
We enumerated all search allocations and compared those with identical total search across environments containing three, five, or ten cues.
Individual search was limited to five cues.
In three-and five-cue environments, the greatest feasible variation in search counts was among the best-performing allocations in every comparison.
In ten-cue environments, this proportion fell to 7.7%, and homogeneous or intermediate allocations often performed better.
Independent validation supported many differences, but the average and maximum accuracy losses from maximal variation were only 0.065 and 0.214 percentage points.
Restricting search to odd numbers of cues reduced these differences.
Search heterogeneity therefore has environment-dependent consequences even when total information acquisition is held constant.
The model provides a theoretical benchmark for investigating how variation in individual information acquisition contributes to collective decisions.
>Introduction
text.formatted: <head n="1." >Introduction</head>

text.text: Decision makers cannot always acquire and process all the information relevant to a choice.
Information acquisition and comparison require time and cognitive resources, and these constraints are central to bounded rationality (Simon, 1955 (Simon, , 1956)).
text.formatted: Information acquisition and comparison require time and cognitive resources, and these constraints are central to bounded rationality <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">(Simon, 1955</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">(Simon, , 1956))</ref>.

text.text: The amount of information people examine also varies.
Process-tracing experiments show that people adjust information acquisition to time pressure and task structure (Payne et al., 1988).
text.formatted: Process-tracing experiments show that people adjust information acquisition to time pressure and task structure <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">(Payne et al., 1988)</ref>.

text.text: Individual differences matter as well: Levin et al. (2000) reported differences in the breadth and depth of information processing associated with need for cognition.
text.formatted: Individual differences matter as well: <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">Levin et al. (2000)</ref> reported differences in the breadth and depth of information processing associated with need for cognition.

text.text: Thus, variation in search is not merely a convenient modeling assumption; it concerns an observable feature of decision making.
When such individuals form a group, a question arises about the consequences of their differences.
Some members may investigate extensively, while others examine only a few cues.
Does this variation improve collective judgment, or would the same total amount of search be better distributed evenly?
We address this question by focusing on diversity, a central contributor to the wisdom-of-crowds effect, and examining one specific form: diversity in the amount of information search.
A fixed-resource comparison makes the question concrete.
Twenty people with a total of sixty cue inspections could each inspect three cues.
Alternatively, ten could inspect one cue each and ten could inspect five, giving the same total: 10 × 1 + 10 ×5 = 60.
Further allocations can combine several search levels.
These groups have the same size and total search, but assemble information into individual judgments differently.
Comparing them separates the effect of allocating search from that of simply acquiring more information.
Our model assigns search counts externally to establish this comparison.
It does not explain how people choose their effort.
Search counts provide an operational measure of information acquisition, rather than a direct measure of time, subjective effort, or monetary cost.

This distinction follows the broader recognition that information-processing demands and decision accuracy must be evaluated together, without treating different measures of effort as interchangeable (Johnson and Payne, 1985).
text.formatted: This distinction follows the broader recognition that information-processing demands and decision accuracy must be evaluated together, without treating different measures of effort as interchangeable <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(Johnson and Payne, 1985)</ref>.

text.text: Aggregating individual judgments can yield accurate collective estimates and decisions.
In Galton's (1907) classic report, the median estimate of an animal's weight closely approximated its actual weight.
text.formatted: In <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">Galton's (1907)</ref> classic report, the median estimate of an animal's weight closely approximated its actual weight.

text.text: Over approximately the past fifteen years, research has examined how social influence, network structure, discussion, and adaptation affect collective accuracy (Lorenz et al., 2011; Becker et al., 2017; Navajas et al., 2018; Almaatouq et al., 2020).
text.formatted: Over approximately the past fifteen years, research has examined how social influence, network structure, discussion, and adaptation affect collective accuracy <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">(Lorenz et al., 2011;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">Becker et al., 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">Navajas et al., 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">Almaatouq et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: These studies show that collective performance depends on how judgments are formed and combined, not merely on gathering more individuals.
Diversity is an important part of this process.
Differences among members can bring together complementary information, perspectives, and approaches (Hong and Page, 2004; Conradt et al., 2013; Fujisaki et al., 2018; de Courson et al., 2021).
text.formatted: Differences among members can bring together complementary information, perspectives, and approaches <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(Hong and Page, 2004;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">Conradt et al., 2013;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">Fujisaki et al., 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">de Courson et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Related research considers cognitive-process diversity, individual heterogeneity in animal groups, stakeholder knowledge, and hybrid human-language-model crowds (Keck and Tang, 2020; Jolles et al., 2020; Jones et al., 2025; Abels and Lenaerts, 2025).
text.formatted: Related research considers cognitive-process diversity, individual heterogeneity in animal groups, stakeholder knowledge, and hybrid human-language-model crowds <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">(Keck and Tang, 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">Jolles et al., 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">Jones et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">Abels and Lenaerts, 2025)</ref>.

text.text: These forms of diversity are distinct, but together motivate investigating which differences contribute to collective performance.
The benefits of diversity do not imply a universal linear relationship between its magnitude and collective accuracy.
More specifically, increasing diversity need not continuously improve performance.

Studies have examined optimal proportions of predictor types and intermediate levels of cognitive diversity (Lamberson and Page, 2012; Aggarwal et al., 2019). Fujisaki et al. (2018) also compared seven mixture proportions of two inference strategies in their first study.
text.formatted: Studies have examined optimal proportions of predictor types and intermediate levels of cognitive diversity <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">(Lamberson and Page, 2012;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">Aggarwal et al., 2019)</ref>. <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">Fujisaki et al. (2018)</ref> also compared seven mixture proportions of two inference strategies in their first study.

text.text: The relevant question is therefore not simply whether a diverse group can outperform a homogeneous one, but how performance changes across feasible compositions in a given environment.
Search amount must also be distinguished from information content.
Members inspecting the same number of cues may inspect different subsets.
Conversely, members inspecting different numbers may reach identical decisions.
Using the cue-based framework of Luan et al. (2012) as a benchmark, we examine differences in search amount while retaining random variation in which cues individuals inspect.
text.formatted: Using the cue-based framework of <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">Luan et al. (2012)</ref> as a benchmark, we examine differences in search amount while retaining random variation in which cues individuals inspect.

text.text: Homogeneity in search counts therefore does not mean that everyone receives identical information.

A central issue in collective intelligence is whether a group benefits more from individually accurate members or from differences among them. Hong and Page (2004) showed how diverse problem solvers can outperform high-ability groups under specified conditions. Luan et al. (2012) examined this diversity-versus-ability question in cue-based decisions.
text.formatted: A central issue in collective intelligence is whether a group benefits more from individually accurate members or from differences among them. <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">Hong and Page (2004)</ref> showed how diverse problem solvers can outperform high-ability groups under specified conditions. <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">Luan et al. (2012)</ref> examined this diversity-versus-ability question in cue-based decisions.

text.text: Their simulations showed that the relative importance of individual accuracy and diversity depended on the distribution of cue predictive strengths: individual accuracy mattered more when these strengths differed substantially, whereas diversity mattered more when their differences were smaller.
Luan et al.'s agents used Take-the-Best or Minimalist.
Both inspect cues sequentially and stop when a cue distinguishes the alternatives, but they differ in search order.
Consequently, a fixed number of available cues does not imply a fixed number of actual inspections.
Their notion of ability concerns individual decision accuracy, not simply how many cues an agent can inspect.

We extend this framework by giving all agents the same search and integration procedure: select cues randomly, inspect the assigned number without early stopping, and combine their contributions with equal weights.
Agents differ in their assigned search counts, not in the form of their integration rule.
These are parameterized variants of a common procedure, rather than a mixture of Take-the-Best and Minimalist.

This modification makes it possible to hold actual total search exactly constant. Stolle et al. (2024) provide a close precedent by studying equal-weight strategies using different numbers of cues in a model with search costs and free riding.
text.formatted: This modification makes it possible to hold actual total search exactly constant. <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">Stolle et al. (2024)</ref> provide a close precedent by studying equal-weight strategies using different numbers of cues in a model with search costs and free riding.

text.text: Our study instead holds group participation and total search constant and enumerates all feasible allocations.
Unlike changing the proportions of two fixed search types, which generally changes mean search, this design compares different distributions of the same search resources.
It identifies the accuracy consequences of redistribution, including any resulting changes in individual accuracy.
We investigated twenty-member groups in environments with three, five, or ten available cues.
Individuals inspected between one and five cues, subject to availability.
Thus, complete individual coverage was possible with three or five cues, but not with ten.
We compared all search allocations sharing the same mean across four cue-strength environments and their pairwise mixtures, using separate discovery and validation samples.
The results revealed an environment-dependent relationship.
With three or five available cues, the greatest feasible variation in search counts was always among the best-performing allocations.
With ten cues, homogeneous or intermediate allocations often performed better, depending on mean search.
These advantages were generally small and became smaller when only odd search counts were permitted.
The study therefore provides a theoretical benchmark for asking how individual search heterogeneity affects collective accuracy under a fixed resource budget.
>Methods
text.formatted: <head n="2." >Methods</head>

text.text: The model links three steps: agents acquire cue information, form independent binary judgments, and combine their judgments by majority vote.
Each group contained twenty agents.
We varied how many cues each agent inspected while keeping the group's total number of inspections identical within each comparison.
The primary outcome was the probability that the collective decision selected the correct alternative.
Each task set contained fifteen objects and all their unordered pairs, giving 15 × 14 /2 = 105 comparisons.
Objects had cue values and a criterion value.
The correct decision selected the object with the larger criterion; agents observed binary cues, not the criterion.
Because the same objects appeared in multiple comparisons, the 105 pairs were not independent observations.
The task set was the unit for estimating simulation uncertainty.
We considered environments containing K = 3, 5, or 10 cues.

Following Luan et al. (2012), four baseline environments differed in how unevenly predictive strength was distributed across cues: large differences (LD), medium differences (MD), small differences (SD), and no differences (ND).
text.formatted: Following <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">Luan et al. (2012)</ref>, four baseline environments differed in how unevenly predictive strength was distributed across cues: large differences (LD), medium differences (MD), small differences (SD), and no differences (ND).

text.text: The environmental label SD is distinct from the standard deviation of individual search counts.
Five-cue environments used the original coefficients.
For three and ten cues, coefficients were interpolated along cue rank while preserving their sum of squares and the noise coefficient.
Consequently, varying K changed both cue availability and the coefficient distribution.
Evaluating several environments follows research showing that the performance of decision procedures depends on task structure (Johnson and Payne, 1985; Payne et al., 1988; Luan et al., 2012).
text.formatted: Evaluating several environments follows research showing that the performance of decision procedures depends on task structure <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(Johnson and Payne, 1985;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">Payne et al., 1988;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">Luan et al., 2012)</ref>.

text.text: To extend this comparison beyond single environments, we examined every pair of the four baselines: LD-MD, LD -SD, LD-ND, MD-SD, MD-ND, and SD-ND.
There were 4 × 3 /2 = 6 pairs.
Each pair was combined at three ratios, 20:80, 50:50, and 80:20, producing 6 ×3 = 18 mixtures.
Together with the four single environments, this yielded 4 +18 = 22 environmental compositions.
A mixture assigned one baseline environment to an entire task set, rather than mixing coefficients within an object.
For example, a 20:80 LD-ND mixture represented a task set drawn from LD with probability 0.2 and ND with probability 0.8.
These comparisons evaluated fixed search allocations across different task distributions; they did not implement temporal adaptation or learning.
Each agent inspected s distinct cues, where s ranged from 1 to m = min(K, 5).
Accordingly, the available search levels were 1-3 when K = 3 and 1-5 when K = 5 or 10.
For each object pair, an agent selected a uniformly random subset of the assigned size.
Cues were not repeated within an agent's comparison, but different agents could inspect overlapping subsets.
Every assigned inspection was completed, so assigned and actual search counts coincided.
For each inspected cue, the agent subtracted the binary value of object B from that of object A, then summed these differences with equal weights.
A positive sum selected A, a negative sum selected B, and a zero sum selected either with probability one-half.
Odd search counts did not eliminate ties because an individual cue difference could be zero.
The group adopted the alternative receiving more votes.
A 10-10 tie was resolved by a separate fair random choice.
Every agent contributed one vote regardless of search amount.
Agents did not observe others' judgments, share cue information, learn cue orderings, or adjust their search counts.
Let n_s denote the number of agents inspecting s cues.
An allocation specified nonnegative integers n_1, ..., n_m summing to twenty.
We enumerated all such vectors, including allocations with no agents at particular search levels.
This is the number of ways to distribute twenty indistinguishable agent counts among m search categories: C(20 + m -1, m -1).
For three categories, C(22, 2) = 231; for five categories, C(24, 4) = 10,626.
Thus, K = 5 and K = 10 each had 10,626 allocations.
Agent identities were irrelevant; exchanging equally configured agents did not create another allocation.
Total search was T = Σ_s s n_s, and mean search was μ = T/20.
Comparisons were restricted to allocations with identical T. Diversity was summarized by the population standard deviation of the twenty search counts.
We identified the smallest and largest feasible standard deviations for each mean.
The allocation attaining the largest value is called the maximum-SD allocation.
The formulas and enumeration details appear in Supplementary Information S1.
Means admitting only one allocation were excluded.
For K = 3, the comparable means ran from 1.10 to 2.90 in steps of 0.05: (2.90 -1.10)/0.05 +1 = 37 means.
For K = 5 or 10, the range was 1.10-4.90, giving 77 means.
Combining these with the 22 environmental compositions produced 37 ×22 = 814 comparison cells for K = 3 and 77 ×22 = 1,694 cells for each larger K.
The resource constraint counted every agent's inspection, including accesses to cues also inspected by others.
It did not fix the number of distinct cues encountered by the group.
Nor did we fix mean individual accuracy.
The allocation manipulation could change individual accuracy, overlap in information, and dependence among errors.
Standard deviation summarized the allocation; it was not manipulated independently of its shape or the proportion of agents with even search counts.
For each K, we generated 20,000 discovery task sets and an independent 20,000 validation task sets.
Within each K and data split, allocations and baseline environments shared underlying continuous cue draws and criterion noise.
Differences between allocations were evaluated on paired task sets.
For each object pair, we calculated response probabilities by averaging over all possible cue subsets and individual tie outcomes.
We then calculated majority-vote accuracy exactly, including group ties, rather than sampling one realized vote per agent.
Task-set accuracy was the mean across its 105 comparisons.
Monte Carlo uncertainty therefore arose primarily from generating a finite collection of task sets.
Supplementary Information S2 provides the conditional probability calculation.
For each mean and environmental composition, discovery data selected a promising nonmaximum-SD allocation.
Validation data evaluated that candidate against the maximum-SD allocation.
Approximate simultaneous Monte Carlo intervals used Gaussian multipliers, with correction across the three K settings for approximately 95% simultaneous coverage.
These intervals concern simulation uncertainty under the specified model, not uncertainty about its empirical assumptions.
The primary outcome was absolute group accuracy.
Loss from the maximum-SD allocation was the highest estimated accuracy within a cell minus its accuracy.
Being among the numerical best included ties; independent validation assessed selected pairwise differences rather than establishing an exact population optimum.
We used a provisional tolerance of 0.1 percentage points, equivalent to 0.001 on the probability scale, to distinguish detectable differences from their magnitude.
This was an interpretive threshold, not an empirically established standard of practical importance.
Sensitivity analyses restricted search to 1, 3, or 5 cues and separately examined within-task-set median dichotomization with five cues.
Post hoc analyses classified the locations of best allocations and compared absolute group accuracy with improvement over the average individual.
Further details appear in S3-S6.
>Results
text.formatted: <head n="3." >Results</head>

text.text: How search diversity affected collective accuracy depended on the number of available cues.
When three or five cues were available, spreading search amounts as unevenly as possible achieved the highest estimated accuracy, sometimes jointly with less dispersed allocations.
When ten cues were available, more even distributions often did better.
We first compare these environments, then examine the size of the differences and the allocations favored in the ten-cue setting.
The maximum-SD allocation was among the best in all 814 three-cue cells and all 1,694 five-cue cells (Table 1).
text.formatted: The maximum-SD allocation was among the best in all 814 three-cue cells and all 1,694 five-cue cells (Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_0">1</ref>).

text.text: In everyday terms, groups combining extensive and limited search could attain the best performance without increasing total search.
This does not mean that any heterogeneous group outperformed every homogeneous group, or that the greatest variation was necessary.
In the five-cue setting, 726 of the 1,694 cells also contained a nonmaximum allocation tied for best.
With ten available cues, the maximum-SD allocation was among the best in 131 of 1,694 cells, or 7.7%.
The remaining 1,694 -131 = 1,563 cells favored another allocation.
Nevertheless, its accuracy loss averaged only 0.065 percentage points and reached a maximum of 0.214 points.
These percentages count the designed mean-by-environment cells equally; they do not estimate how frequently particular environments occur outside the model.
In the ten-cue setting, the discovery-selected alternative outperformed the maximum-SD allocation beyond the simultaneous error margin in 1,478/1,694 = 87.2% of cells.
This supports the selected alternatives' advantages on independent tasks, without implying that every selected candidate was uniquely optimal.
Using the provisional 0.1-point tolerance, the maximum-SD allocation was classified as within tolerance in 1,179/1,694 = 69.6% of cells.
Losses exceeded tolerance in 507/1,694 = 29.9%.
The remaining 8/1,694 = 0.5% were unresolved because their intervals crossed the threshold.
These categories exhaust the comparisons: 1,179 + 507 +8 = 1,694.
Frequent detectable differences therefore coexisted with generally close performance.
Supplementary Information S3 reports the classification.
Post hoc comparisons at integer means clarified which allocations were favored with ten cues.
At mean search two, all twenty agents inspecting two cues was numerically best.
At mean three, the best allocation comprised one agent inspecting one cue, twelve inspecting two, and seven inspecting five.
At mean four, it comprised six agents inspecting two cues, one inspecting three, and thirteen inspecting five (Table 2).
text.formatted: At mean four, it comprised six agents inspecting two cues, one inspecting three, and thirteen inspecting five (Table <ref type="table">2</ref>).

text.text: The same respective allocations were best across all 22 environmental compositions.
At mean two, the homogeneous group used twenty two-cue judgments.
The maximum-SD alternative instead contained fifteen one-cue agents and five five-cue agents, again totaling 15 × 1 + 5 ×5 = 40 inspections.
Equalizing search across voters was therefore better than concentrating it in a smaller subset at this mean.
At means three and four, however, the best groups still contained seven and thirteen fivecue agents, respectively.
The preferred allocation was neither uniformly homogeneous nor uniformly concentrated across search budgets.
At mean three, the best allocation used 1 × 1 + 12 × 2 + 7 ×5 = 60 inspections, exactly matching both twenty three-cue agents and the maximum-SD allocation of ten one-cue and ten five-cue agents.
Its superiority therefore reflected redistribution, not more search.
It retained some extensive search while raising the search amounts of many other voters.
The LD accuracy advantages over maximum SD were approximately 0.158, 0.026, and 0.003 percentage points at means two, three, and four, respectively.

Note.
Each listed allocation was numerically best across the 22 environmental compositions.
SD is the population standard deviation of search counts.
Means three and four favored intermediate SD, meaning strictly between the feasible minimum and maximum, not necessarily near their midpoint.
Classification was post hoc.
Across the 1,563 cells where maximum SD was not best, 22 favored zero SD, 440 favored the smallest feasible SD at a noninteger mean, and 1,101 favored an intermediate SD: 22 + 440 + 1,101 = 1,563.
The 440 minimum-SD cases are not evidence favoring additional heterogeneity.
At mean 1.6, for example, eight one-cue and twelve two-cue agents give 8 +24 = 32 inspections, or 32/20 = 1.6.
This is the most even feasible allocation, although its SD is positive.
The results do not establish a uniform inverted-U relationship.
Restricting search to 1, 3, or 5 cues preserved the five-cue result: maximum SD remained among the best in every cell.
With ten cues, its frequency increased from 7.7% to 53.4%.
Mean and maximum losses fell to 0.021 and 0.089 percentage points, and all 814 restricted comparisons were within the 0.1-point tolerance.
The restriction changed both the allocations and comparable means, so it did not isolate parity or tie resolution alone.
Five-cue results also persisted under within-set median dichotomization (S5).
Finally, absolute accuracy and improvement over individual performance could favor different allocations.
In a post hoc ten-cue, ND example with mean search 1.6, the best group's accuracy was 70.498%, versus 70.284% under maximum SD.
Yet maximum SD produced the larger group-minusindividual improvement: 12.045 versus 11.766 percentage points.
Its individual baseline was lower (58.239% versus 58.732%).
Thus, a larger aggregation gain did not imply a more accurate final decision (S6).
The distribution of information search affected collective accuracy even when group size and total search were identical.
With three or five available cues, the greatest feasible variation in search amounts was always among the best-performing allocations.
With ten cues, more even allocations often did better: complete homogeneity was best at mean two, whereas intermediate variation was best at means three and four.
Many advantages survived independent validation, but their magnitudes were small.
The central finding is therefore an environment-dependent effect of search heterogeneity, not a general prescription to maximize or minimize diversity.
This result has a methodological implication for agent-based modeling.
Such models can represent individual heterogeneity, but which differences to include remains a substantive choice (Reeves et al., 2022).
text.formatted: Such models can represent individual heterogeneity, but which differences to include remains a substantive choice <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">(Reeves et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Assigning every agent a common search amount treats information acquisition as homogeneous, even if other attributes vary.
Human research indicates that acquisition differs across both decision contexts and individuals (Payne et al., 1988; Levin et al., 2000).
text.formatted: Human research indicates that acquisition differs across both decision contexts and individuals <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">(Payne et al., 1988;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">Levin et al., 2000)</ref>.

text.text: Our comparison shows that replacing a distribution of search counts with its mean can alter predicted collective performance.
Search heterogeneity is therefore a candidate explanatory feature, rather than simply additional descriptive detail.
The contribution also extends the diversity-versus-ability question.

Previous work establishes that differences among members can support collective intelligence, and that the balance between diversity and individual accuracy depends on the task (Hong and Page, 2004; Luan et al., 2012).
text.formatted: Previous work establishes that differences among members can support collective intelligence, and that the balance between diversity and individual accuracy depends on the task <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(Hong and Page, 2004;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">Luan et al., 2012)</ref>.

text.text: Here, individual accuracy was not an independently assigned ability parameter.
It emerged from search amount, sampled cues, and a shared decision rule.
Holding total search constant revealed how reallocating information acquisition changes the judgments available for aggregation.
The question becomes how a boundedly rational group distributes the work that produces its individual judgments.
The model makes an important feature of this process explicit: information is aggregated twice.
First, inspected cues become an individual's binary decision.
Second, those decisions become equal votes.
Giving one member more information necessarily removes inspections from other members, but does not increase the informed member's voting weight.
Concentrating search within a few judgments therefore need not be equivalent to spreading it across many voters.
The same total resource can enter different points in the collective decision process, producing different outcomes without changes in membership or voting rules.
The contrast between cue counts suggests a possible explanation.
With three or five available cues, some agents can inspect the entire cue set.
With ten cues and a five-cue search limit, even the most extensive search remains incomplete.
Concentrating resources may then provide less benefit relative to the cost of leaving other voters with little information.
This interpretation fits the results, but complete coverage was not isolated experimentally: changing cue count also changed coefficient distributions.
Varying the individual search ceiling within a fixed environment would directly test this explanation.
Complete coverage would still involve binary cues and criterion noise, rather than perfect knowledge.
Search-count diversity should not be equated with diversity of answers or independent errors.
Even equally resourced agents can consult different cues, while differently resourced agents can agree.
Shared task difficulty can also associate errors across tasks without communication.
Research on forecasting composition and cognitive-process diversity highlights the importance of both individual accuracy and error dependence (Lamberson and Page, 2012; Keck and Tang, 2020).
text.formatted: Research on forecasting composition and cognitive-process diversity highlights the importance of both individual accuracy and error dependence <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">(Lamberson and Page, 2012;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">Keck and Tang, 2020)</ref>.

text.text: Our manipulation can affect both.
Direct measurement of information overlap and joint errors would help explain which changes account for the observed advantages, beyond their description by search-count SD.
The feasible allocation set also matters.
Restricting search to odd counts reduced the disadvantages of maximum variation, while integer constraints made zero variation impossible at noninteger means.
Together with the homogeneous optimum at mean two, these findings rule out interpreting every departure from maximum SD as evidence for a universal intermediate optimum.

Intermediate advantages are already known in other diversity research (Aggarwal et al., 2019); the present contribution is the controlled comparison of search distributions under an exactly matched resource budget.
text.formatted: Intermediate advantages are already known in other diversity research <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Aggarwal et al., 2019)</ref>; the present contribution is the controlled comparison of search distributions under an exactly matched resource budget.

text.text: SD describes these distributions but does not determine their full shape or informational consequences.
Effect size is equally important.
The average ten-cue loss from maximum SD was 0.065 percentage points, and most comparisons fell within the provisional 0.1-point tolerance.
The findings establish differences among allocations without implying large practical penalties for choosing a highly dispersed one.
Moreover, an allocation can improve more over its average member while remaining less accurate in absolute terms.
Studies of collective intelligence should distinguish the accuracy of the final decision from the size of its improvement over an individual baseline.
Our model provides a theoretical reference point for empirical tests, not an estimate of how human groups currently allocate search.
It specifies the consequences of redistribution when twenty agents use fixed search counts, equal-weight integration, and independent majority voting.
Search is externally assigned; stopping rules, strategic incentives, and social learning are not modeled.
Those processes can shape which compositions arise and persist (de Courson et al., 2021; Jia et al., 2026).
text.formatted: Those processes can shape which compositions arise and persist <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(de Courson et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">Jia et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Their omission makes the present comparison interpretable, while defining the conditions under which its predictions should be tested.
A direct experiment could give groups the same total number of information accesses and vary their allocation before independent voting.
Recording inspected cues, acquisition time, and individual decisions would test whether the modeled resource distribution translates into comparable information use.
Departures from the benchmark could then be investigated by changing cue weighting, stopping rules, or social information.
Interaction and network adaptation would be subsequent extensions, rather than explanations of the current results (Almaatouq et al., 2020).
text.formatted: Interaction and network adaptation would be subsequent extensions, rather than explanations of the current results <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Almaatouq et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: More generally, collective intelligence depends not only on the information available to a group, but on how its acquisition is distributed and how that information is transformed into a collective decision.
